common_name: Shearer's Lady Fern (Black-Green Groundcover Painted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or spore-grown starts in spring in humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade; this is an apomictic triploid that spreads very slowly, so give it an uncrowded spot where it won't be smothered by faster neighbors while it establishes.

directions: Shearer's Lady Fern forms a low, slowly spreading clump of lustrous black-green fronds, making it more a groundcover than an upright specimen fern. Native to valley and streamside woodlands of China, Japan, and Korea up to 6,000 feet elevation, it was brought into Western cultivation from spore material supplied by fern authority John Mickel from Japan and has only recently reached specialty US nurseries in quantity. Grow it in part sun to light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich soil, where its dense dark foliage reads almost black against companion plantings; it also tolerates drier shade once established. Use it as a small-scale groundcover, living-wall filler, or container specimen in a woodland setting.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Lemon Cream Japanese Painted Fern (Gold-Blotched Variegated Painted Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in open shade or with only a couple hours of morning sun, since both variegation and vigor are strongest without harsh afternoon exposure.

directions: Lemon Cream carries the lacy, arching habit typical of Japanese painted fern but adds irregular lemon-cream blotching across the green fronds, a variegation pattern that starts subtly in spring and becomes much more pronounced by late summer and fall. It was named and brought into the US nursery trade by plantsman Barry Yinger from Asian collecting stock, and performs best in open or morning-sun shade, where the pale patterning shows most clearly without scorching. It tolerates drier shade once established, making it useful in woodland borders, rain gardens, and mixed shade containers where a brighter accent among green-leaved companions is wanted. Protect new spring growth from slugs while fronds are unfurling.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden

common_name: Pearly White Japanese Painted Fern (Chalky White Low-Arching Painted Fern)
scientific_name: Athyrium niponicum 'Pearly White' (syn. Anisocampium niponicum 'Pearly White')

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, and bait or trap for slugs and snails early since the pale, tender fronds are especially attractive to them.

directions: Pearly White stands out among Japanese painted fern selections for foliage that is overwhelmingly chalky white rather than the more typical silver-and-burgundy mix, with slightly rounded, downward-curving pinnae that give the whole frond a soft, pillowy look. It forms a low, arching clump that spreads gradually from a slow-colonizing rhizome rather than running aggressively, and works well as a pale accent against darker-leaved hostas or ferns in a shaded border. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, since strong light quickly bleaches and burns the delicate white tissue. Watch closely for slug and snail damage, which disfigures the pale fronds more visibly than it would a green-leaved cultivar.

common_name: Okanum Eared Lady Fern (Creamy-Crozier Painted-Relative Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in evenly moist, humus-rich woodland soil in part to full shade; established clumps hold their foliage later into fall frosts than Japanese painted fern before finally collapsing.

directions: This selection of the eared lady fern sends up new croziers in a ghostly creamy yellow, cloaked in lustrous broad black scales, before unfurling into symmetrical, vase-shaped fronds. Mature foliage pairs rounded, lime-to-olive-green pinnae with deep burgundy stipes, a color combination distinct from the silver-toned Japanese painted fern cultivars it is often grown alongside. The selection traces to spore material sourced through English commercial fern grower Ray Coughlin and remains uncommon in US specialty nurseries. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part to full shade, where it holds attractive color later into autumn than most of its Athyrium relatives.

common_name: Green Hans Kinki Wood Fern (Wide-Fronded Asian Evergreen Wood Fern)

planting.note: Plant divisions or spore-grown starts in spring in light shade in evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil; this species is slow to bulk up, so expect several years before it forms the substantial clump it's known for.

directions: Green Hans is a selection of the little-grown Kinki wood fern, distinguished by unusually wide, dark green evergreen fronds that give it a bolder, denser presence than most Dryopteris in cultivation. It was spore-propagated from material collected by plantsman Hans Hansen in Guizhou, China, and introduced through Juniper Level Botanic Garden's Asian plant-exploration program, remaining scarce outside specialty collector nurseries. Grow in light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich soil; growth is slow at first, but plants eventually form a dense, deer-resistant clump suited to a woodland shade border. Native across China, Japan, and Korea, it is hardy through USDA zone 7 with reliable winter protection of the crown in colder parts of its range.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
